elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement for convenience.
elements.evidence: Section 14.2.2 expressly permits PB as Customer to terminate for convenience at any time.

elements.element: Customer termination for convenience requires 30 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The clause requires 90 days' prior notice, not 30 days.

elements.element: Customer's termination notice must be written.
Customer receives a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees upon termination for convenience.
elements.evidence: No pro-rata refund obligation appears. The clause instead imposes an early-termination payment, and the absence of prepaid fees is not demonstrated.

elements.element: Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term.
elements.evidence: The added language permits SFJ's convenience termination to become effective only at the end of the then-current term.

elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement for convenience.
elements.evidence: Section 14.2.2 expressly permits PB as Customer to terminate for convenience at any time.

elements.element: Customer termination for convenience requires 60–90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The clause requires 90 days' prior written notice, which is within the permitted range.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee does not exceed three months' fees.
elements.evidence: The cap is three months' “Development Costs,” not three months' fees. Nothing establishes that Development Costs are equivalent to, or no broader than, fees.
The added operative sentence expressly grants SFJ as Vendor a termination-for-convenience right.

elements.element: Vendor termination for convenience may be effective only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: The added sentence states that termination may be effective only at the end of the then-current term.

elements.element: Vendor termination for convenience requires 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The added sentence requires 90 days' prior written notice to PB.

result.reason: The preferred position fails because the notice period is 90 rather than 30 days and no pro-rata refund is provided. The fallback also fails strictly because its fee cap uses three months' Development Costs rather than three months' fees. The drafting is not minimal and does not preserve unrelated commercial terms because the blanket statement that Sections 14.2.6 and 14.2.10 are “limited accordingly” modifies separate change-of-control and JSC-disagreement termination rights. That formulation is also imprecise and sits uneasily with those sections' existing “at any time” language.
